stem: In a RAG pipeline, which statement about a text embedding is accurate?

options.text: It is a one-hot vector over the vocabulary, with a 1 for every word that appears in the text and 0 everywhere else
options.why: That describes a sparse bag-of-words vector. Embeddings are dense: almost every dimension is non-zero and no dimension stands for one word.

options.text: A fixed-length vector of numbers that places texts with similar meaning close together
options.why: Correct: the model maps any input to the same number of dimensions, and training pulls semantically related texts together in that space.

options.text: Its length grows with the length of the text, so a long chunk gets a longer vector than a short query
options.why: A given model always outputs the same dimensionality, which is what makes query and chunk vectors comparable at all.

options.text: It stores the token ids of the text, so the chunk is read back from the vector when the prompt is built
options.why: An embedding is not a token list. It is a learned summary used for similarity search; you keep the chunk text separately to put into the prompt.

explanation: An embedding model turns a piece of text into a dense vector with a fixed number of dimensions, for example 1,536 for OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small`. Training places texts that mean similar things near each other, so nearest-neighbour search over chunk vectors finds semantically related chunks even without shared words. Interviewers open with this to check you know embeddings are dense, fixed-length and geometric, not sparse word counts.

stem: With the same embedding model, a 5-word query and a 400-word chunk are turned into vectors with the same number of dimensions.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the output size is a property of the model (for example 1,024 or 1,536), not of the input length.

options.text: False
options.why: Dimensionality does not depend on input length. If it did, a query vector could not be compared with a chunk vector at all.

explanation: Encoders pool their token representations into one vector of fixed size, so every input from one model lands in the same space with the same length. Input length matters in a different way: text beyond the model's maximum input tokens is truncated and never represented.

stem: What is the cosine similarity of the vectors `[3, 4]` and `[4, 3]`? Give the value to two decimal places.
explanation: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the lengths: (3x4 + 4x3) / (5 x 5) = 24 / 25 = 0.96. Both vectors have length 5 and point in nearly the same direction, so the similarity is high.

stem: You index all chunks with embedding model A. Why must user queries also be embedded with model A (same model and version)?

options.text: Because the vector database rejects query vectors that were produced by a different provider
options.why: Most stores only check dimensionality. A same-sized vector from another model is accepted silently, which is exactly why this bug is dangerous.

options.text: Because model A has a larger context window, so only model A can read the long user queries
options.why: Queries are short; context window is not the reason. The issue is that the two spaces are not aligned.

options.text: Each model learns its own vector space, so cross-model similarity is meaningless
options.why: Correct: dimensions in two independently trained models have no shared meaning, so cross-model scores do not reflect relevance.

options.text: Because cosine similarity is only defined when both vectors were computed on the same hardware
options.why: Hardware has nothing to do with it. Cosine works on any two vectors; the result is only meaningful if they share a space.

explanation: Every embedding model defines its own coordinate system. Query and document vectors are only comparable when they come from the same model, and the same version, since a retrained model is a different space. Mixing models usually produces near-random rankings without any error message, because the dimensions often match.

stem: The query vector is `q = [1, 0]`. Order these document vectors by **cosine** similarity to `q`, highest first.
explanation: Cosine only looks at direction: `[0.96, 0.28]` scores 0.96, `[0.8, 0.6]` scores 0.8, `[12, 16]` scores 12/20 = 0.6 and `[5, 12]` scores 5/13 = 0.385. A raw dot product would rank them almost the other way round (12, 5, 0.96, 0.8) because it rewards vector length, which is why you normalise or use cosine unless the model was trained for dot-product scoring.

stem: Which two statements describe how a bi-encoder embedding model is used for retrieval? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each document is re-encoded whenever a new query arrives so that its vector reflects that query
options.why: That would make retrieval cost grow with corpus size on every query, which is exactly what bi-encoders avoid.

options.text: The model outputs one vector per token, and every query token is compared with every document token
options.why: That describes multi-vector late interaction (ColBERT-style), not a single-vector bi-encoder.

options.text: Document vectors can be computed once at indexing time and reused for every future query
options.why: Correct: because documents are encoded without the query, their vectors are precomputed and stored, so query time needs one encoding plus a vector search.

options.text: The query and each document are encoded independently, each into its own vector
options.why: Correct: a bi-encoder never sees the query and the document together; it produces one vector per text.

options.text: The model reads each query-document pair together and outputs a relevance score for that pair
options.why: That is a cross-encoder. It is more accurate per pair but must run once per candidate at query time, so it is used for reranking, not first-stage retrieval.

explanation: Sentence-BERT popularised the bi-encoder (siamese) set-up: one encoder maps each text to a single vector, and relevance is a cheap similarity such as cosine. The corpus side is precomputed, so a query costs one model call plus a nearest-neighbour search. The price is that query and document never interact inside the model, which is why a cross-encoder reranker is often added on top.

stem: You embed 2,000-token chunks with Cohere `embed-english-v3.0`, whose maximum input is 512 tokens, and leave `truncate` at its default. What happens?

options.text: The API returns an error for every chunk longer than 512 tokens
options.why: That is the behaviour of `truncate: NONE`. The default is `END`, which trims instead of failing.

options.text: The model splits each chunk into four parts and averages their vectors
options.why: The API does not chunk and pool for you. Splitting text to fit the model is your chunker's job.

options.text: The vector gets longer to make room for the extra tokens
options.why: Output dimensionality is fixed per model (1,024 here); input length never changes it.

options.text: Only roughly the first 512 tokens are embedded; the rest of each chunk is discarded and cannot be matched
options.why: Correct: the default `END` drops tokens from the end until the input fits, so facts in the tail are invisible to vector search.

explanation: Cohere's `truncate` parameter defaults to `END` (discard the end of the input until it fits); `START` discards the beginning and `NONE` returns an error instead. Silent truncation is a classic RAG bug: the chunk text in the prompt is complete, but only its head was embedded, so questions about the tail never retrieve it. Size chunks to the embedding model's input limit.

stem: Match each similarity or distance measure to the description that fits it.

options.text: Cosine similarity
options.why: Depends only on the angle between vectors; higher means more similar.

options.text: Dot product
options.why: Grows with vector length as well as angle; equals cosine on unit vectors.

options.text: Euclidean (L2) distance
options.why: Straight-line distance; lower means more similar.

options.text: Hamming distance
options.why: Counts differing bits; used to compare binary-quantised embeddings.

prompts.text: Two vectors pointing the same way score the same no matter how long they are
A document vector with a large norm can outrank a better-aligned short one
Ranking puts the smallest value first
Comparing 1-bit-per-dimension codes cheaply with XOR and popcount

explanation: Cosine normalises away magnitude; dot product does not, so on unnormalised vectors longer vectors win; Euclidean is a distance, so smaller is better (on unit vectors it ranks exactly like cosine, since squared L2 = 2 - 2 x cosine); Hamming distance is what binary-quantised embeddings use for fast first-pass search.

stem: Query `q = [1, 0]`. Document vectors (not normalised): `d1 = [0.9, 0.1]`, `d2 = [3, 3]`. Which document ranks first under dot product, and which under cosine similarity?

options.text: `d2` under dot product (3.0 vs 0.9) and `d1` under cosine (0.994 vs 0.707)
options.why: Correct: dot product rewards the large norm of `d2`, while cosine only sees that `d1` is far better aligned.

options.text: `d1` under both, because it points almost exactly along the query
options.why: Cosine agrees, but dot product is 0.9 for `d1` and 3.0 for `d2`, so `d2` wins on dot product.

options.text: `d2` under both, because it has the larger values in every dimension
options.why: Cosine ignores magnitude: `d2` sits at 45 degrees to the query (cosine 0.707) while `d1` is at about 6 degrees (0.994).

options.text: `d1` under dot product (it is better aligned) and `d2` under cosine (it is longer)
options.why: That reverses both results. Compute them: dot gives 0.9 vs 3.0; cosine gives 0.994 vs 0.707.

explanation: Dot product = |q||d|cos(theta), so with unnormalised vectors the length of `d` leaks into the score. Cosine divides the length out. If your model was trained for cosine and you store raw vectors in a dot-product index, long or high-norm vectors get an unfair boost. Normalise to unit length and the two measures become identical.

stem: A teammate swaps the query encoder to a newer model that also outputs 1,024 dimensions, but leaves the chunk index built with the old model untouched. No errors appear. What do you expect?

options.text: Slightly better results, because the newer model understands queries better
options.why: Query understanding cannot help if the query vector lives in a different space from the stored vectors.

options.text: Near-random rankings, with relevant chunks no longer reliably on top
options.why: Correct: the two models' spaces are not aligned, so similarity scores stop tracking relevance even though every call succeeds.

options.text: Identical results, because the dimensionality matches
options.why: Matching dimensions only means the maths runs. It says nothing about whether dimension 17 means the same thing in both models.

options.text: The vector store re-embeds the stored chunks automatically on the next query
options.why: Stores hold vectors, not your model; they cannot re-embed anything for you.

explanation: Equal dimensionality is a coincidence, not compatibility. This failure is silent: searches return results with plausible-looking scores, so it is usually caught by retrieval metrics dropping or by users. Query and corpus must be re-embedded together whenever the model or its version changes.

stem: You use an E5-family model (for example `intfloat/multilingual-e5-large`) for passage retrieval. How should inputs be prepared?

options.text: Send raw text for both queries and passages; prefixes are optional style hints
options.why: The model card says the prefixes are how the model was trained and that leaving them out degrades performance.

options.text: Prefix both queries and passages with `passage: ` so they share one space
options.why: Using the passage prefix on queries throws away the query/passage distinction the model learned for retrieval.

options.text: Prefix queries with `query: ` and passages with `passage: `
options.why: Correct: this asymmetric task uses different prefixes for the two sides, exactly as the model was trained.

options.text: Prefix passages only, since queries are too short to need one
options.why: Queries need their `query: ` prefix too; a missing prefix on either side is a common silent quality bug.

explanation: The E5 model card answers this in its FAQ: use `query: ` and `passage: ` for asymmetric retrieval such as open-domain QA, and use `query: ` on both sides for symmetric tasks such as semantic similarity or paraphrase retrieval. Without the prefixes you get performance degradation, not an error.

stem: With Cohere Embed v3 or later, which `input_type` should you send when embedding the chunks you store in the vector database?

options.text: `search_query`
options.why: That value is for the user's query at search time. Using it for stored chunks breaks the asymmetry the model expects.

options.text: `classification`
options.why: That is for vectors fed to a text classifier, not for a search index.

options.text: `clustering`
options.why: That is for vectors run through a clustering algorithm, not for retrieval.

options.text: `search_document`
options.why: Correct: Cohere documents `search_document` for embeddings stored in a vector database for search.

explanation: `input_type` is required for Embed v3 and newer. Documents go in with `search_document` and queries with `search_query`; the model produces slightly different vectors for the two roles so that short questions match the passages that answer them. Sending the wrong value does not raise an error, it quietly lowers retrieval quality.

stem: Two unit-length embedding vectors have cosine similarity 0.5. What is the **squared** Euclidean distance between them?
explanation: For unit vectors, squared L2 distance = |a|^2 + |b|^2 - 2a.b = 2 - 2 x cosine = 2 - 1 = 1. That identity is why cosine similarity and Euclidean distance give exactly the same ranking once vectors are normalised: one is a decreasing function of the other.

stem: OpenAI's embeddings guide states that its embeddings are normalised to length 1. Which two consequences follow? (Choose two.)

options.text: Cosine similarity and Euclidean distance produce identical rankings
options.why: Correct: squared L2 = 2 - 2 x cosine for unit vectors, so sorting by one is sorting by the other in reverse.

options.text: Shortening a vector by slicing off its tail keeps it at length 1
options.why: A sliced vector is shorter than 1; OpenAI's docs say to normalise again if you truncate manually.

options.text: Cosine similarity can be computed with a plain dot product
options.why: Correct: for unit vectors the denominator of cosine is 1, so dot product and cosine are the same number.

options.text: All similarity scores will be spread evenly between -1 and 1
options.why: Normalisation fixes the range, not the distribution; many models put most scores in a narrow band.

options.text: Similarity scores from these models can be compared directly with scores from any other normalised model
options.why: Unit length does not align two different spaces; scores are only meaningful within one model.

explanation: Normalised vectors make the choice of metric mostly a performance detail: dot product is the cheapest way to get cosine, and L2 ranks identically. OpenAI recommends cosine and notes the choice of distance function typically does not matter much. The catch is manual truncation, which breaks unit length.

stem: You are shortlisting embedding models for a new RAG system. Which three factors should drive the choice? (Choose three.)

options.text: The model's rank on the overall MTEB average alone, since it already reflects every use case
options.why: The MTEB authors found no single method dominates across tasks; an average hides your task and domain.

options.text: Languages and deployment constraints such as on-prem hosting, licence and data residency
options.why: Correct: a model you are not allowed to call or host, or that does not cover your languages, is out regardless of its score.

options.text: Maximum input tokens compared with your chunk sizes
options.why: Correct: text past the input limit is truncated and never represented, so the limit must fit your chunks.

options.text: Retrieval quality on queries and documents from your own domain
options.why: Correct: performance on your data is the deciding signal; public benchmarks only shortlist.

options.text: Whether the model has the most dimensions available, since more dimensions always retrieve better
options.why: More dimensions cost storage and latency and do not guarantee better retrieval; shortened OpenAI embeddings can beat larger older ones.

explanation: A good answer lists domain fit measured on your own queries, languages, maximum input length, dimensions (storage and latency), price, latency and throughput, and hosting or licence constraints. Benchmarks such as MTEB are a starting filter, not a decision.

stem: Order these per-vector storage footprints from smallest to largest.

options.text: 256-dimension float32 vector
1,024-dimension float32 vector
1,024-dimension binary vector (1 bit per dimension)
1,536-dimension int8 vector

explanation: Binary: 1,024 / 8 = 128 bytes. 256 float32: 256 x 4 = 1,024 bytes. 1,536 int8: 1,536 bytes. 1,024 float32: 4,096 bytes. Precision per dimension can matter more than the dimension count: quantising to int8 cuts float32 storage by 4x and binary by 32x, while Matryoshka-style truncation cuts the number of dimensions.

stem: If chunk similarity of 0.80 is a good relevance cut-off with one embedding model, you can keep the same 0.80 cut-off after switching to a different embedding model.

options.text: True
options.why: Scores are not calibrated across models, so a cut-off tuned for one model is meaningless for another.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: every model has its own score distribution. The E5 model card, for example, notes its cosine scores cluster in a narrow high band because of a low training temperature.

explanation: Absolute similarity values depend on how a model was trained. The multilingual E5 card explains that scores bunching high is expected and that relative order matters more than absolute values. Any threshold must be re-tuned on labelled data after a model change.

stem: Why is a model's position on the public MTEB leaderboard not enough to choose an embedding model for your RAG system?

options.text: A many-task public average may not reflect your domain and queries
options.why: Correct: the MTEB authors found no single method dominates across tasks, so you still need to test on your own data.

options.text: Because MTEB only contains English classification tasks and no retrieval tasks
options.why: MTEB covers 8 task types including retrieval, 58 datasets and 112 languages in the original paper.

options.text: Because MTEB scores are measured with dot product, which is invalid for normalised vectors
options.why: The metric is not the issue; on unit vectors dot product and cosine are the same thing.

options.text: Because leaderboard models cannot be used through APIs
options.why: Many listed models are API models; availability is not why the leaderboard is insufficient.

explanation: MTEB (Muennighoff et al., 2022) spans 8 embedding tasks, 58 datasets and 112 languages, and its own conclusion is that no particular embedding method dominates across all tasks. Use it to shortlist, then measure retrieval on labelled queries from your corpus, and weigh cost, latency, dimensions and hosting.

stem: You must store 10 million chunk embeddings of 1,536 dimensions. Roughly how much raw vector storage does float32 need, and how much does int8 need?

options.text: About 15 GB as float32 and about 2 GB as int8
options.why: 15 GB is the int8 figure and about 2 GB (1.92 GB) is the binary figure; float32 is four times the int8 size.

options.text: About 61 GB as float32 and about 15 GB as int8
options.why: Correct: 10M x 1,536 x 4 bytes = 61.44 GB; int8 uses 1 byte per dimension, 15.36 GB.

options.text: About 6 GB as float32 and about 1.5 GB as int8
options.why: That is off by a factor of ten; redo 10,000,000 x 1,536 x 4 bytes.

options.text: About 123 GB as float32 and about 31 GB as int8
options.why: Those are the figures for 3,072-dimension vectors, double the stated size.

explanation: Raw size = vectors x dimensions x bytes per dimension. Index structures and metadata add more on top, so treat this as the floor. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can reason about the cost of dimensions and precision before you pick a model.

stem:
This search returns the *least* similar chunks. What is the bug?

```python
import numpy as np

def search(q, D, k):
    # D: (n, d) matrix of unit-normalised chunk vectors
    q = q / np.linalg.norm(q)
    scores = D @ q
    idx = np.argsort(scores)[:k]
    return idx, scores[idx]
```

options.text: The query must not be normalised, because cosine needs raw magnitudes
options.why: Normalising the query only scales every score by the same factor, so the ranking is unchanged; it is not the bug.

options.text: `D @ q` computes Euclidean distance, so smaller really is better
options.why: `D @ q` is a dot product; with unit vectors that is cosine similarity, where larger is better.

options.text: `np.argsort` sorts ascending, so `[:k]` takes the k lowest scores; sort on `-scores` (or take the last k reversed)
options.why: Correct: with scores `[0.9, 0.1, 0.5]`, `argsort(scores)[:2]` is `[1, 2]`, while `argsort(-scores)[:2]` is `[0, 2]`.

options.text: `scores[idx]` returns the scores in the wrong order but the indices are right
options.why: The indices themselves are the k worst matches, so the scores alongside them are the k worst too.

explanation: `np.argsort` returns indices that sort ascending. For similarity (larger is better) you need descending order: `np.argsort(-scores)[:k]`, or `np.argpartition` for large n followed by sorting just the k winners. This is one of the bugs interviewers plant in a live-coding cosine search.

stem: In a take-home in-memory index, `search` uses `idx = np.argpartition(-scores, k)[:k]`. A test with 3 documents and `k=3` crashes. What is the right fix?

options.text: Wrap the call in `try/except` and return an empty list when it fails
options.why: That hides the problem: a caller asking for 3 of 3 documents would get nothing instead of everything.

options.text: Replace `argpartition` with `argsort(scores)[:k]`
options.why: That swaps a crash for a silent bug: ascending order returns the worst matches.

options.text: Pad the corpus with zero vectors until it has more than k rows
options.why: Zero vectors would be returned as results and, after normalising, produce NaN scores.

options.text: Clamp `k = min(k, n)`, partition on `k - 1`, then sort the k winners
options.why: Correct: `argpartition` raises `ValueError` when `kth` equals n; using `kth = k - 1` with a clamped k works for every `1 <= k <= n`.

explanation: `np.argpartition(a, kth)` needs `kth` to be a valid index (`0 <= kth < n`), so `kth = 3` on 3 rows raises `ValueError: kth(=3) out of bounds (3)`. A robust search also returns `[]` for an empty corpus or a zero query vector, and sorts the partitioned winners with a deterministic tie-break (for example by index).

stem: You are asked to implement `build(docs)` and `search(query, k)` for a small in-memory cosine index. Which three choices belong in a correct, efficient implementation? (Choose three.)

options.text: Re-embed all documents inside `search` so their vectors are always fresh
options.why: That makes every query cost a full corpus embedding; documents are embedded once at build time.

options.text: Normalise every document vector once in `build`, so `search` only needs one matrix-vector product
options.why: Correct: precomputing unit vectors turns cosine into a dot product and avoids recomputing norms on every query.

options.text: Loop over documents in Python and compute cosine one pair at a time to keep memory low
options.why: A vectorised `D @ q` is orders of magnitude faster and the memory is just one score per document.

options.text: Guard against zero-norm vectors so normalising does not divide by zero and produce NaN scores
options.why: Correct: an empty or degenerate input can embed to all zeros; NaN scores silently break sorting.

options.text: Use `argpartition` to get the top k in linear time, then sort only those k by score
options.why: Correct: full sorting is O(n log n); partition plus sorting k items is cheaper for large n.

explanation: The interview version of this task checks vectorisation, normalising once, correct descending top-k, and edge cases: empty corpus, k larger than the corpus, zero vectors and ties. Verified behaviour: `np.argpartition(-s, k - 1)[:k]` then a sort of those k gives the right top k for any `1 <= k <= n`.

stem: You want to compare three embedding models for an internal knowledge base. Which evaluation gives you a trustworthy answer?

options.text: Build a labelled set of real user queries with their relevant chunks, embed the corpus with each model, and compare recall@k on that set
options.why: Correct: the same queries, corpus and chunking for every model isolate the model's effect on retrieval.

options.text: Pick the model with the highest MTEB retrieval average, since it was evaluated on many datasets
options.why: Public averages may not reflect your domain or query style; they shortlist, they do not decide.

options.text: Ask an LLM to rate how 'semantic' each model's vectors look on a handful of sample sentences
options.why: Impressions on a few sentences say little about whether the right chunks come back for real queries.

options.text: Compare the average cosine similarity each model gives between queries and their top result
options.why: Score scales differ between models, so a higher average similarity does not mean better retrieval.

explanation: A model comparison should hold everything else fixed (corpus, chunking, query set, k) and measure retrieval against relevance labels from your domain. Raw similarity values cannot be compared across models because each model has its own score distribution. Add cost, latency and dimensions to the decision once quality is known.

stem: Constraints: documents are in Hindi and English, the data may not leave your servers, and your chunks are up to 450 tokens. Which embedding choice fits every constraint?

options.text: OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large` with `dimensions=1024`
options.why: A strong model, but it is a hosted API, which breaks the data-must-stay-on-premises constraint.

options.text: An open-weights multilingual model such as `intfloat/multilingual-e5-large`, self-hosted
options.why: Correct: it covers about 100 languages from XLM-RoBERTa, runs on your own hardware, and its 512-token limit fits 450-token chunks.

options.text: Cohere `embed-english-v3.0` called over a dedicated private network link to the provider
options.why: It is English-only, so Hindi text is out of scope, and it is still an external API.

options.text: An English-only open-source sentence model fine-tuned on your English documents
options.why: Self-hosted, but English-only training leaves the Hindi half of the corpus poorly represented.

explanation: Write down hard constraints first (languages, hosting, input length), eliminate models that break any of them, then benchmark the survivors on your own queries. The multilingual E5 card states 100-language support with possible degradation on low-resource languages and truncation at 512 tokens.

stem: Why can you shorten an OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large` vector to 256 dimensions with the `dimensions` parameter and keep useful quality, when chopping an ordinary embedding model's vector to its first 256 values usually wrecks retrieval?

options.text: Because OpenAI compresses the vector with PCA on the server for each request
options.why: The docs describe shortening by removing numbers from the end, not a per-request PCA.

options.text: Because the leading dimensions of any embedding always carry the most information
options.why: That is only true when training makes it so; an ordinary model spreads information across all dimensions.

options.text: It was trained Matryoshka-style, so leading prefixes are usable embeddings
options.why: Correct: Matryoshka Representation Learning trains nested prefixes to work at several sizes, so truncation keeps most of the meaning.

options.text: Because 256 dimensions is the true size of the model and the rest is zero padding
options.why: The other dimensions carry information; that is why the full vector scores higher than shortened ones.

explanation: Matryoshka Representation Learning (Kusupati et al., 2022) trains one embedding so that its coarse prefixes are good representations too. OpenAI's guide says you can shorten embeddings by removing numbers from the end without losing their concept-representing properties, and that on MTEB a 256-dimension `text-embedding-3-large` vector still outperforms a full 1,536-dimension `text-embedding-ada-002` vector.

stem: To save space you slice stored `text-embedding-3-small` vectors to their first 512 values yourself instead of using the `dimensions` parameter, and keep using a dot-product index. Recall drops more than you expected. What did you miss?

options.text: Slicing changes the model's tokenizer, so queries must be re-tokenised
options.why: Slicing a stored vector has nothing to do with tokenisation.

options.text: You must also slice the query vector to its last 512 values
options.why: Query and documents must use the same leading dimensions; taking the last values mixes different coordinates.

options.text: Dot-product indexes require at least 1,024 dimensions
options.why: There is no such requirement; dimension counts are a storage and quality trade-off.

options.text: Sliced vectors are no longer unit length; re-normalise them after slicing
options.why: Correct: OpenAI's docs say a manually truncated embedding must be normalised again; the slice keeps only part of the vector's length.

explanation: Embeddings returned at full size are unit length, but a prefix of a unit vector is shorter than 1 (for a random 3,072-dimension unit vector, the first 256 values have norm of about 0.27). Different chunks lose different amounts of length, so dot-product scores get distorted. The `dimensions` parameter returns a properly normalised shortened vector; if you slice yourself, apply L2 normalisation afterwards.

stem: Your support docs are in English. Users ask in Hindi. Which approach lets a Hindi query retrieve the matching English passage with **no translation step at query time**?

options.text: Embed both sides with one multilingual embedding model
options.why: Correct: a shared multilingual space places a Hindi question near the English passage that answers it.

options.text: Keep one index per language and route each query to the index for its own language
options.why: A Hindi query would only search Hindi documents, so the English passages are never considered.

options.text: Use BM25 over the English documents with the raw Hindi query
options.why: Keyword matching needs shared tokens; Hindi and English text share almost none.

options.text: Embed documents with an English model and queries with a Hindi model of the same dimension
options.why: Two separately trained models produce incompatible spaces, even at equal dimensionality.

explanation: Cross-lingual retrieval works when one model embeds every language into a common space, as multilingual models trained on parallel data do. Alternatives are translating at ingest (store everything in one language) or translating queries at search time, which adds latency and translation errors.

stem: Storing only embeddings instead of the raw text is enough to protect sensitive content, because an embedding cannot be turned back into readable text.

options.text: True
options.why: Inversion attacks can recover much of the original text from embeddings, so vectors need the same protection as the text.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Morris et al. (2023) recovered 92% of 32-token inputs exactly from their embeddings and extracted full names from embeddings of clinical notes.

explanation: Embeddings leak information. The vec2text work ("Text Embeddings Reveal (Almost) As Much As Text") showed a multi-step inversion method that reconstructs most short inputs exactly. Treat a vector store holding sensitive documents with the same access control and encryption as the source data.

stem: An E5-style asymmetric model works well for question-to-passage search. You now also need duplicate-question detection (question-to-question similarity) with the same model. How should you prefix the inputs?

options.text: `query: ` on one question and `passage: ` on the other
options.why: Asymmetric prefixes are for a short query against a long passage; two questions are the same kind of text.

options.text: `query: ` on both questions
options.why: Correct: the E5 card says to use the `query: ` prefix for symmetric tasks such as semantic similarity and paraphrase retrieval.

options.text: `passage: ` on both questions, because both are full sentences
options.why: The card recommends `query: ` for symmetric tasks, not `passage: `.

options.text: No prefixes, because prefixes only matter for retrieval
options.why: The model was trained with prefixes on every input; dropping them degrades all uses.

explanation: Asymmetric retrieval compares a short query with a longer passage, so models learn different roles for the two sides. Symmetric tasks compare like with like. E5's guidance: `query:`/`passage:` for asymmetric retrieval, `query:` on both sides for symmetric similarity, and `query:` for features used in clustering or linear probing.

stem: Match each Cohere Embed `input_type` value with the job it is for.

options.text: `search_document`
options.why: Vectors stored in a vector database for search.

options.text: `search_query`
options.why: Vectors for queries run against that database.

options.text: `classification`
options.why: Vectors passed to a text classifier.

options.text: `clustering`
options.why: Vectors grouped by a clustering algorithm.

prompts.text: Embedding 50,000 help-centre chunks during nightly indexing
Embedding the user's question when they hit search
Embedding tickets so a classifier can label them by department
Grouping feedback comments into themes without labels

explanation: Cohere asks you to state the job because the model produces vectors tuned to it. For RAG the pair that matters is `search_document` at indexing time and `search_query` at query time; mixing them up quietly lowers retrieval quality.

stem: You must cut vector-store memory for 100 million embeddings and can afford a little extra latency. Using binary quantisation with a rescoring step, what does the Hugging Face embedding-quantisation study report?

options.text: A 4x memory reduction with no change in retrieval quality
options.why: 4x is the int8 figure; binary gives 32x.

options.text: A 32x memory reduction but recall falls to about half, so it is unusable for RAG
options.why: The study reports about 92.5% retained without rescoring and about 96% with it, far from half.

options.text: A 32x memory reduction, with about 96% of retrieval performance kept when the top candidates are rescored with the float32 query
options.why: Correct: binary stores 1 bit per dimension, and rescoring the shortlist with the full-precision query recovers most of the loss.

options.text: An 8x reduction, because each dimension is stored in 4 bits
options.why: Binary quantisation thresholds each dimension to a single bit (above 0 becomes 1).

explanation: Binary quantisation thresholds normalised embeddings at 0 and compares codes with Hamming distance; storage drops 32x. Retrieving a larger shortlist with binary codes and rescoring it with the float32 query kept about 96% of retrieval performance in the study (about 92.5% without rescoring). Int8 scalar quantisation is 4x smaller and keeps about 97% (99% with rescoring) using calibrated per-dimension ranges.

stem: A 1,024-dimension embedding is binary-quantised (1 bit per dimension). How many bytes does one vector take? Type a number.
explanation: 1,024 bits / 8 bits per byte = 128 bytes, compared with 4,096 bytes for the float32 vector: the 32x reduction that binary quantisation is known for.

stem: Budget: about 20 GB of RAM for raw vectors. Corpus: 10 million chunks. Your model natively outputs 1,536 float32 dimensions. Which option fits the budget with the least expected quality loss?

options.text: Keep 1,536 float32 dimensions and buy time with a smaller top-k
options.why: That needs 61.44 GB of raw vectors; top-k has no effect on storage.

options.text: Binary-quantise to 1 bit per dimension (about 1.9 GB) and skip rescoring
options.why: It fits easily, but binary without rescoring loses more quality (about 92.5% retained in the study) than int8.

options.text: Keep float32 but use the first 512 dimensions of the model's output without re-normalising
options.why: 20.48 GB is just over budget, and slicing without re-normalising distorts dot-product scores.

options.text: Quantise to int8 at 1,536 dimensions (about 15.4 GB)
options.why: Correct: it fits, and int8 scalar quantisation typically keeps about 97% of retrieval quality, more with rescoring.

explanation: Compute first: 10M x 1,536 x 4 B = 61.44 GB (float32), x 1 B = 15.36 GB (int8), / 8 = 1.92 GB (binary). Then pick the least lossy option that fits. Interviewers want the arithmetic plus awareness of what each compression costs in recall.

stem: Retrieval is weak on your company's jargon, so you decide to fine-tune an open embedding model. Which plan for the data and the success check is sound?

options.text: Train on (query, relevant passage) pairs, adding hard negatives where you have them, and confirm with recall@k on held-out real domain queries
options.why: Correct: contrastive pairs or triples teach the model which passage answers which query, and a held-out set shows whether retrieval actually improved.

options.text: Continue next-token pre-training on raw domain documents and judge success by lower perplexity
options.why: Perplexity measures language modelling, not whether queries land next to the right passages.

options.text: Train a classifier on document categories and judge success by classification accuracy
options.why: Category accuracy says little about ranking the specific passage that answers a question.

options.text: Train on (query, passage) pairs and judge success by the training loss going down
options.why: Training loss can fall while held-out retrieval stays flat or overfits; you must test on unseen queries.

explanation: Sentence-Transformers' `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss` accepts (anchor, positive) pairs, (anchor, positive, negative) triples or longer n-tuples, and uses other in-batch items as negatives. Hard negatives (passages that look relevant but are not) sharpen the boundary. Success is measured on held-out domain queries with retrieval metrics, compared against the base model.

stem: You fine-tune with `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, which treats the other passages in the batch as negatives. Your training set has many near-duplicate FAQ entries. What risk should you address, and how?

options.text: Duplicates make the loss negative; switch to a mean-squared-error loss
options.why: The loss does not go negative; the problem is wrong labels, not the loss's sign.

options.text: Duplicates in a batch become false negatives; use a no-duplicates sampler
options.why: Correct: Sentence-Transformers recommends `BatchSamplers.NO_DUPLICATES` so in-batch negatives do not duplicate the anchor or positive.

options.text: Duplicates slow training; reduce batch size to 1 to avoid collisions
options.why: Batch size 1 removes every in-batch negative, which is the main learning signal of this loss.

options.text: Duplicates are harmless because in-batch negatives are ignored when similar
options.why: The loss does not know they are similar; it pushes them apart as if they were wrong answers.

explanation: With in-batch negatives, every other positive in the batch is a negative for this anchor. If a paraphrase of the true answer sits in the same batch, the model is trained to push away a correct match (a false negative). Deduplicate or use the no-duplicates sampler. Larger batches give more negatives; the cached variant of the loss allows larger batches without extra memory.

stem: Before fine-tuning an embedding model for weak domain retrieval, which two checks or cheaper fixes should come first? (Choose two.)

options.text: Try other off-the-shelf models, including domain or multilingual ones, on the same labelled queries
options.why: Correct: swapping models is cheaper than training one and sometimes closes the gap.

options.text: Fine-tune on the test queries so the improvement is guaranteed to show
options.why: Training on the evaluation set leaks answers and makes the measured gain meaningless.

options.text: Lower the similarity threshold until the right chunk appears
options.why: That lets in more noise without moving the right chunk up the ranking.

options.text: Confirm the misses are really embedding failures by checking whether the right chunks exist and are well formed
options.why: Correct: bad parsing or chunking often looks like a weak model; fine-tuning cannot retrieve text that was never indexed properly.

options.text: Raise the vector dimensionality of the current model, since more dimensions capture jargon
options.why: You cannot add dimensions to a trained model; dimensions are fixed by training.

explanation: Fine-tuning has a real cost: collecting pairs, training, hosting a custom model, and re-embedding the corpus every time the model changes. First rule out data problems and try existing models on a labelled set. Fine-tune when a measured gap remains, and always keep a held-out set that the training data never touched.

stem: During an embedding-model upgrade, a job re-embedded 60% of the chunks with the new model before it was stopped. Both models output 1,024 dimensions, so search keeps working. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing: the new model is better, so the 60% just retrieves better
options.why: Query vectors come from one model; the chunks from the other model are scored in an incompatible space.

options.text: Only latency suffers, because the index stores two kinds of vectors
options.why: The vectors are the same size and cost the same to search; correctness is what breaks.

options.text: Each query vector is compatible with only one of the two groups, so the other group gets meaningless scores and the merged ranking is corrupted
options.why: Correct: vectors from two models are not comparable even at equal dimensionality, so one population is ranked effectively at random.

options.text: The 40% of old vectors are simply skipped by the store
options.why: The store cannot tell vectors from different models apart; it scores all of them.

explanation: A mixed index is a silent correctness bug. The safe approach is to build a complete new index with the new model alongside the old one, evaluate it, switch queries over in one step and keep the old index for rollback; the operational rollout belongs to production practice, but the reason it is needed is this incompatibility.

stem: You are replacing your embedding model. Which three things must be redone, not just the query encoder? (Choose three.)

options.text: Re-run the retrieval evaluation on your labelled query set before switching
options.why: Correct: you need evidence the new model is better on your data, and a baseline to compare against.

options.text: Re-train the LLM that generates the answer
options.why: The generator reads chunk text, not vectors, so it does not depend on the embedding model.

options.text: Re-tune any similarity thresholds and score-based cut-offs
options.why: Correct: score distributions differ between models, so old thresholds no longer mean the same thing.

options.text: Re-embed the entire corpus with the new model
options.why: Correct: old document vectors are incompatible with new query vectors.

options.text: Delete the old index before building the new one
options.why: Keep the old index until the new one is proven, so you can roll back.

explanation: Changing the embedding model invalidates every stored vector and every number tuned against its scores (thresholds, hybrid weights calibrated on raw scores). It does not touch the generator. Plan the switch as a full rebuild and measure before cutting over.

stem: A bank's assistant must answer Hindi and English questions over a corpus that is mostly English with some Hindi circulars. Constraints: no translation or extra LLM call on the query path, Hindi circulars must stay searchable in their original text, and a Hindi question must be able to retrieve an English policy. Which design satisfies all three?

options.text: Translate all Hindi circulars into English at ingest and use an English-only model
options.why: Hindi originals are no longer what is indexed, which breaks the second constraint, and Hindi queries would still need translating.

options.text: One index per language, routing each query by detected language
options.why: A Hindi question would never reach the English policies, which breaks the third constraint.

options.text: An English-only model with LLM translation of Hindi queries before embedding
options.why: It works for cross-lingual lookup but adds an LLM call on the query path, which is ruled out.

options.text: One index built with a multilingual embedding model, used for queries too
options.why: Correct: the shared space keeps Hindi text as-is, needs no query-time translation, and lets Hindi questions match English passages.

explanation: Each multilingual strategy has a cost: translating at ingest loses the original text and depends on translation quality; per-language indexes lose cross-lingual recall; query-time translation adds latency and errors. A multilingual embedding model is the option that meets these three constraints; you still evaluate it per language, since low-resource languages can be weaker.

stem: A team embeds a corpus that is half Hindi (Devanagari) and half English with an English-only embedding model. English queries work; Hindi queries return poor results. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The model never learned Hindi, so Hindi texts get vectors that do not capture their meaning
options.why: Correct: an English-only model cannot place Hindi questions near the Hindi passages that answer them.

options.text: The vector store does not support Unicode metadata
options.why: Metadata encoding does not change the vectors; the embeddings themselves are the problem.

options.text: Hindi text splits into more tokens per sentence, so it needs a much larger top-k to surface the right chunk
options.why: More candidates do not help if the vectors do not encode Hindi meaning in the first place.

options.text: Cosine similarity is undefined for non-Latin scripts
options.why: Cosine works on numbers; the script only matters to the model that produced them.

explanation: Language coverage is a hard filter when choosing a model. Cohere's model page, for example, lists `embed-english-v3.0` as English only and `embed-multilingual-v3.0` as covering over 100 languages. Pick a model trained on every language in your corpus and evaluate each language separately.

stem: Order the steps for choosing between candidate embedding models on your own corpus.

options.text: Label which chunks answer each query
Weigh the quality results against cost, latency, dimensions and hosting constraints
Embed the same chunked corpus with each candidate, using each model's required query/document input types
Sample real user queries (or realistic ones) from the target domain
Run the queries and compute recall@k and a rank-aware metric per model

explanation: Ground truth comes first: real queries and labelled relevant chunks. Then hold the corpus and chunking constant, embed with each candidate (respecting prefixes or `input_type`), and measure. Only then trade quality off against price, latency, storage and hosting. Public leaderboards can shortlist candidates before step one but cannot replace it.

stem: Match each production symptom to its most likely embedding-side cause.

options.text: Query vectors from a new model, chunk vectors from the old one
options.why: Model or version mismatch between query and corpus.

options.text: Text beyond the model's maximum input was cut off
options.why: Silent truncation at embedding time.

options.text: Unnormalised vectors searched with dot product
options.why: Vector length inflates scores.

options.text: A model trained with a low contrastive temperature
options.why: Scores bunch in a narrow high band.

prompts.text: Answers in the second half of long chunks are never retrieved
Right after a deploy, relevance looks random though no errors were logged
Long, generic chunks keep outranking short, precise ones
Almost every chunk scores between 0.75 and 0.9, relevant or not

explanation: Each symptom points at a different fix: re-embed with one model, chunk to fit the input limit, normalise vectors (or use cosine), and rely on ranking or a tuned threshold rather than absolute scores. The E5 card explains the narrow score band as expected behaviour from its 0.01 InfoNCE temperature.

stem: You serve 100 million chunks and need low latency and low memory, but you cannot accept a big recall loss. Your model is Matryoshka-trained. Which design uses that property best?

options.text: Use only the last 256 dimensions, because they hold the finest detail
options.why: Matryoshka training makes the leading prefix usable on its own; the tail alone is not a valid embedding.

options.text: Search with a short prefix of each vector (for example 256 dimensions) to get a candidate shortlist, then rescore the shortlist with full-length vectors
options.why: Correct: coarse nested prefixes are cheap for the first pass, and full vectors restore precision on a small candidate set.

options.text: Store vectors at full length and randomly sample dimensions per query to save compute
options.why: Random subsets do not align with the nested structure the model learned and vary between queries.

options.text: Average the first and second halves of each vector into one half-length vector
options.why: This mixes coordinates in a way the model was never trained for; truncation is the supported operation.

explanation: The Matryoshka paper reports up to 14x real-world speed-ups for large-scale retrieval by using smaller embeddings, which is the shortlist-then-rescore (adaptive retrieval) pattern. The same idea works with binary codes for the first pass and float vectors for rescoring.

stem: You generate synthetic training queries with an LLM from your documents to fine-tune an embedding model, and then evaluate on more synthetic queries from the same generator. The fine-tuned model scores much higher, but users see little change. What is the most likely flaw?

options.text: The fine-tuned model has too many dimensions
options.why: Fine-tuning does not change the output dimensionality; this does not explain the gap.

options.text: Synthetic queries cannot be used for training at all
options.why: They are a common, useful way to create training pairs; the flaw is evaluating only on the same distribution.

options.text: The test queries mimic the generator, not real users
options.why: Correct: the model learned to match synthetic phrasing; a held-out set of real queries is needed to measure real gains.

options.text: The model must be fine-tuned with a cross-encoder loss instead
options.why: The loss choice is not the issue; the evaluation set is.

explanation: Synthetic data is fine for training, but an evaluation built from the same generator rewards learning the generator's quirks (copying document phrasing, predictable question shapes). Keep a held-out set of real queries, or at least queries written independently, and compare the base and fine-tuned models on it.

stem: Which two statements about combining Matryoshka truncation and quantisation are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Any embedding model can be truncated to its first 64 dimensions with little loss, as long as you quantise afterwards
options.why: Quantisation does not repair truncation damage; only Matryoshka-trained models tolerate short prefixes.

options.text: A first pass on compressed vectors followed by rescoring a shortlist with fuller vectors recovers much of the lost quality
options.why: Correct: both the quantisation study and the Matryoshka paper rely on shortlist-and-rescore to keep quality.

options.text: Int8 scalar quantisation needs no calibration because every model's values lie in [-1, 1] evenly
options.why: Ranges are estimated from a calibration set of embeddings, per dimension, to set the buckets.

options.text: Truncation reduces the number of dimensions, while quantisation reduces the bytes per dimension, so their savings multiply
options.why: Correct: for example 256 dimensions at int8 is 256 bytes versus 6,144 bytes for 1,536 float32 dimensions.

options.text: Binary quantisation works without any normalisation or thresholding choice
options.why: Binary codes come from thresholding each dimension (at 0 for normalised embeddings); the threshold is part of the method.

explanation: Dimensions and precision are separate levers. Truncation needs a model trained for it (Matryoshka); quantisation needs a scheme (int8 with calibration ranges, or binary thresholding). Both trade some recall for memory and speed, and rescoring a shortlist with fuller vectors is the standard way to buy most of it back.
